short: Rome's first new circuit of walls in over 600 years, a response to invasion during the third-century crisis.
full:
Emperor Aurelian ordered a new defensive circuit around Rome in 271 CE, after an Alamannic and Juthungi invasion had reached northern Italy two years earlier and exposed a city that had relied on its distance from any frontier rather than fortification since the fourth century BCE. The brick-faced concrete wall eventually ran about 19 kilometres, enclosing roughly 13.7 square kilometres and standing some 6 metres high with square towers at regular intervals, incorporating existing structures such as the Pyramid of Cestius and stretches of aqueduct into its line to save labour.

Most of the circuit was finished by Aurelian's death in 275, and his successor Probus completed the remainder. The walls marked a symbolic break: for the first time since the early Republic, Rome itself needed defending rather than merely its frontiers. Later strengthened under Maxentius and again under Honorius around 401–403, the circuit proved effective enough that much of it still stands, and it defined the city's boundary through the medieval period and into the nineteenth century.
